prompt: Determine all complex numbers $\lambda$ for which there exist a positive integer $n$ and a real $n\times n$ matrix $A$ such that $A^2=A^T$ and $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$.

solutions.title: $A^4=A$, plus explicit examples
solutions.body:
**Necessity.** From $A^2=A^T$,
$$A^4=(A^2)^2=(A^T)^2=(A^2)^T=(A^T)^T=A .$$
If $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, then $\lambda v=Av=A^4v=\lambda^4v$, so $\lambda^4=\lambda$, i.e. $\lambda(\lambda^3-1)=0$. Hence
$$\lambda\in\Big\{0,\ 1,\ \tfrac{-1+i\sqrt3}{2},\ \tfrac{-1-i\sqrt3}{2}\Big\}.$$

**Sufficiency.** The $1\times1$ matrices $(0)$ and $(1)$ satisfy $A^2=A^T$ and have eigenvalues $0$ and $1$. Let $R$ be the rotation by $-120^\circ$:
$$R=\begin{pmatrix}-\frac12&\frac{\sqrt3}2\\-\frac{\sqrt3}2&-\frac12\end{pmatrix}.$$
Then $R^2$ is the rotation by $-240^\circ$, i.e. by $+120^\circ$, which is $R^{-1}=R^T$ (rotations are orthogonal). Its eigenvalues are $e^{\pm2\pi i/3}=\frac{-1\pm i\sqrt3}2$. (The block matrix $\operatorname{diag}(0,1,R)$ realises all four values at once.)

**Answer:** $\lambda\in\left\{0,\,1,\,\frac{-1+i\sqrt3}2,\,\frac{-1-i\sqrt3}2\right\}$, the roots of $\lambda^4=\lambda$. ∎

prompt:
Let $f\colon\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ be a differentiable function, and suppose that there exists a constant $L>0$ such that
$$\big|f'(x)-f'(y)\big|\le L|x-y|$$
for all $x,y$. Prove that
$$\big(f'(x)\big)^2<2Lf(x)$$
holds for all $x$.
answer: $f(x+h)\le f(x)+f'(x)h+\frac L2h^2$; take $h=-f'(x)/L$ to get $0<f(x+h)\le f(x)-\frac{f'(x)^2}{2L}$.

solutions.title: Integrate the Lipschitz bound
solutions.body:
$f'$ is Lipschitz, hence continuous, so we may integrate it. Fix $x$ and let $d=f'(x)$; we show $f(x)>\frac{d^2}{2L}$. If $d=0$ this holds as $f(x)>0$.

If $d>0$: for $t\ge0$, $f'(x-t)\ge d-Lt$, which is positive for $0\le t<d/L$. Hence
$$f(x)>f(x)-f\Big(x-\frac dL\Big)=\int_0^{d/L}f'(x-t)\,dt\ge\int_0^{d/L}(d-Lt)\,dt=\frac{d^2}{2L},$$
where the first inequality uses $f>0$.

If $d<0$: similarly $f'(x+t)\le d+Lt=-(|d|-Lt)$, so
$$f(x)>f(x)-f\Big(x+\frac{|d|}L\Big)=\int_0^{|d|/L}\big(-f'(x+t)\big)dt\ge\int_0^{|d|/L}(|d|-Lt)\,dt=\frac{d^2}{2L}.$$
In all cases $f'(x)^2<2Lf(x)$. ∎

solutions.title: Quadratic upper bound (descent lemma)
solutions.body:
For any $x,h$, by the fundamental theorem of calculus ($f'$ is continuous),
$$f(x+h)-f(x)-f'(x)h=\int_0^1\big(f'(x+sh)-f'(x)\big)h\,ds\le\int_0^1Ls|h|\cdot|h|\,ds=\frac L2h^2 .$$
Choose $h=-\frac{f'(x)}L$. Then
$$0<f(x+h)\le f(x)-\frac{f'(x)^2}{L}+\frac{f'(x)^2}{2L}=f(x)-\frac{f'(x)^2}{2L},$$
so $f'(x)^2<2Lf(x)$. ∎

prompt:
For any positive integer $m$, denote by $P(m)$ the product of positive divisors of $m$ (e.g. $P(6)=36$). For every positive integer $n$ define the sequence
$$a_1(n)=n,\qquad a_{k+1}(n)=P(a_k(n))\quad(k=1,2,\dots,2016).$$
Determine whether for every set $S\subseteq\{1,2,\dots,2017\}$, there exists a positive integer $n$ such that the following condition is satisfied:

*For every $k$ with $1\le k\le2017$, the number $a_k(n)$ is a perfect square if and only if $k\in S$.*

solutions.title: Powers of two and a 2-adic lemma
solutions.body:
**Yes.** We take $n=2^{w_1}$. Since $P(2^w)=1\cdot2\cdot4\cdots2^w=2^{w(w+1)/2}$, we get $a_k(n)=2^{w_k}$ with
$$w_{k+1}=T(w_k),\qquad T(w)=\frac{w(w+1)}2,$$
and $2^{w}$ is a perfect square iff $w$ is even. So we need $w_1\ge0$ such that $w_k$ is even exactly for $k\in S$ ($1\le k\le2017$).

**Lemma.** If $j\ge1$ and $c\equiv b+2^j\pmod{2^{j+1}}$, then $T(c)\equiv T(b)+2^{j-1}\pmod{2^j}$.

*Proof.* Write $c-b=2^j u$ with $u$ odd. Then
$$T(c)-T(b)=\frac{(c-b)(c+b+1)}{2}=2^{j-1}\,u\,(2b+1+2^ju).$$
Both $u$ and $2b+1+2^ju$ are odd, so $T(c)-T(b)=2^{j-1}\cdot(\text{odd})\equiv2^{j-1}\pmod{2^j}$. $\square$

**Corollary.** Let $(b_k)$, $(c_k)$ follow the recursion $x_{k+1}=T(x_k)$ with $c_1=b_1+2^m$ ($m\ge1$). Applying the Lemma $k-1$ times, $c_k\equiv b_k+2^{m-k+1}\pmod{2^{m-k+2}}$ for $k=1,\dots,m+1$. Hence $c_k\equiv b_k\pmod2$ for $k\le m$, while $c_{m+1}\equiv b_{m+1}+1\pmod2$.

**Construction.** By induction on $m=1,\dots,2017$ we find a start value whose sequence has the right parity at positions $1,\dots,m$. For $m=1$ take $w_1=0$ if $1\in S$ and $w_1=1$ otherwise. Given a start $b_1$ that works for positions $1..m$: if $b_{m+1}$ already has the right parity keep it; otherwise use $c_1=b_1+2^m$, which by the Corollary keeps the parities at positions $1..m$ and flips position $m+1$. After $m=2017$ we have the desired $w_1$, and $n=2^{w_1}$ works.

**Answer: Yes.** ∎

prompt: There are $n$ people in a city, and each of them has exactly 1000 friends (friendship is always symmetric). Prove that it is possible to select a group $S$ of people such that at least $n/2017$ persons in $S$ have exactly two friends in $S$.
answer: Choose $S$ randomly, each person independently with probability $p=\frac3{1001}$. A person is in $S$ with exactly two friends in $S$ with probability $q=\binom{1000}2p^3(1-p)^{998}>\frac{27\cdot1000\cdot999}{2\cdot1001^3}e^{-3}>\frac1{2017}$, so the expected number of such persons exceeds $n/2017$.

solutions.title: Random selection
solutions.body:
Let $d=1000$ and $0<p<1$. Put each person into $S$ independently with probability $p$. For a fixed person $v$, the events "$v\in S$" and "exactly two of $v$'s $d$ friends are in $S$" are independent, so
$$\Pr\big(v\in S\text{ and }v\text{ has exactly two friends in }S\big)=q:=p\binom d2p^2(1-p)^{d-2}.$$
Let $X$ be the number of persons in $S$ having exactly two friends in $S$. By linearity of expectation $\mathbb E[X]=nq$, so some choice of $S$ has $X\ge nq$. It suffices to show $q>\frac1{2017}$ for a suitable $p$.

Take $p=\frac3{d+1}$ (this maximises $q$). Then $1-p=\frac{d-2}{d+1}$ and
$$q=\frac{27\,d(d-1)}{2(d+1)^3}\Big(\frac{d-2}{d+1}\Big)^{d-2}=\frac{27\,d(d-1)}{2(d+1)^3}\Big(1+\frac3{d-2}\Big)^{-(d-2)}>\frac{27\,d(d-1)}{2(d+1)^3}\,e^{-3},$$
using $(1+\frac xm)^m<e^x$. With $d=1000$: $\frac{d(d-1)}{(d+1)^3}=\frac{999000}{1003003001}>0.000996$, and $e^3<20.1$, so
$$q>\frac{27\cdot0.000996}{2\cdot20.1}>0.000668>\frac1{2017}\approx0.000496 .$$
Hence there is a set $S$ in which at least $nq>\frac n{2017}$ persons have exactly two friends in $S$. ∎

prompt:
Let $k$ and $n$ be positive integers with $n\ge k^2-3k+4$, and let
$$f(z)=z^{n-1}+c_{n-2}z^{n-2}+\dots+c_0$$
be a polynomial with complex coefficients such that
$$c_0c_{n-2}=c_1c_{n-3}=\dots=c_{n-2}c_0=0.$$
Prove that $f(z)$ and $z^n-1$ have at most $n-k$ common roots.
answer: Let $M$ be the $n$-th roots of unity and $A=\{z\in M:f(z)\ne0\}$. For each $\eta\in M$, $\sum_{z\in M}z^2f(z)f(\eta z)=n\eta^{n-1}\ne0$, so $\eta=a/b$ with $a,b\in A$. Hence $|A|(|A|-1)\ge n-1>(k-1)(k-2)$, so $|A|\ge k$.

solutions.title: Every root of unity is a ratio of non-roots
solutions.body:
Let $M=\{z:z^n=1\}$ ($n$ distinct points) and $A=\{z\in M:f(z)\ne0\}$. The common roots of $f$ and $z^n-1$ form $M\setminus A$, so we must prove $|A|\ge k$. Put $c_{n-1}=1$.

**Claim.** For every $\eta\in M$ there are $a,b\in A$ with $a=\eta b$.

Recall $\sum_{z\in M}z^m=n$ if $n\mid m$ and $0$ otherwise. Then
$$\sum_{z\in M}z^2f(z)f(\eta z)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}c_jc_\ell\eta^\ell\sum_{z\in M}z^{j+\ell+2}.$$
Here $2\le j+\ell+2\le2n$, so $n\mid j+\ell+2$ only when $j=\ell=n-1$ or $j+\ell=n-2$. Thus the sum equals
$$n\Big(c_{n-1}^2\eta^{n-1}+\sum_{j=0}^{n-2}c_jc_{n-2-j}\eta^{n-2-j}\Big)=n\eta^{n-1}\ne0,$$
using the hypothesis $c_jc_{n-2-j}=0$. Hence some $b\in M$ has $f(b)\ne0$ and $f(\eta b)\ne0$; take $a=\eta b$. $\square$

**Counting.** For $\eta\ne1$ the pair in the Claim has $a\ne b$. So the map $(a,b)\mapsto ab^{-1}$ from ordered pairs of distinct elements of $A$ onto $M\setminus\{1\}$ is surjective, and
$$|A|(|A|-1)\ge n-1\ge k^2-3k+3.$$
If $|A|\le k-1$, then $|A|(|A|-1)\le(k-1)(k-2)=k^2-3k+2$, a contradiction. Therefore $|A|\ge k$, and $f$ and $z^n-1$ have at most $n-k$ common roots. ∎

prompt:
Let $f\colon[0,+\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be a continuous function such that $\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)=L$ exists (it may be finite or infinite). Prove that
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1f(nx)\,dx=L.$$
answer: $\int_0^1f(nx)\,dx=\frac1n\int_0^nf$, and the averages $\frac1t\int_0^tf$ tend to $L$ (split off a fixed initial piece, or use L'Hôpital's rule with $F(t)=\int_0^tf$, $F'=f\to L$).

solutions.title: Split off an initial interval
solutions.body:
Substituting $t=nx$, $\displaystyle\int_0^1f(nx)\,dx=\frac1n\int_0^nf(t)\,dt$.

**$L$ finite.** Let $\varepsilon>0$ and choose $K$ with $|f(t)-L|<\frac\varepsilon2$ for $t\ge K$. Let $C=\int_0^K|f-L|$ (finite, $f$ is continuous). For $n>K$,
$$\left|\frac1n\int_0^nf-L\right|\le\frac1n\int_0^K|f-L|+\frac1n\int_K^n|f-L|\le\frac Cn+\frac\varepsilon2<\varepsilon$$
as soon as $n>\max(K,2C/\varepsilon)$.

**$L=+\infty$.** Let $M$ be real; choose $K\ge0$ with $f(t)>M+1$ for $t\ge K$, and let $C=\int_0^K f-K(M+1)$. For $n>K$,
$$\frac1n\int_0^nf\ge\frac1n\Big(\int_0^Kf+(n-K)(M+1)\Big)=M+1+\frac Cn>M$$
as soon as $n>|C|$. So the integrals tend to $+\infty$.

**$L=-\infty$.** Apply the previous case to $-f$. ∎

solutions.title: L'Hôpital's rule
solutions.body:
Let $F(t)=\int_0^tf$. Since $f$ is continuous, $F$ is differentiable with $F'=f$. For $t>0$, $\int_0^1f(tx)\,dx=\frac{F(t)}t$.

The denominator $t$ tends to $+\infty$, and $\frac{F'(t)}{(t)'}=f(t)\to L$. The version of L'Hôpital's rule for a denominator tending to $\infty$ (which needs no assumption on the numerator and allows $L=\pm\infty$) gives
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{F(t)}t=L .$$
In particular, along $t=n$, $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1f(nx)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{F(n)}n=L$. ∎

prompt:
Let $p(x)$ be a nonconstant polynomial with real coefficients. For every positive integer $n$, let
$$q_n(x)=(x+1)^np(x)+x^np(x+1).$$
Prove that there are only finitely many numbers $n$ such that all roots of $q_n(x)$ are real.
answer: If all roots of $\sum a_ix^i$ (degree $m$) are real then $a_{m-1}^2-2a_ma_{m-2}=a_m^2\sum w_i^2\ge0$. For $q_n$ the top three coefficients give $B_n^2-2A_nC_n=-a^2n^2+O(n)\to-\infty$.

solutions.title: Sum of squares of the roots
solutions.body:
**Lemma.** If $g(x)=a_mx^m+a_{m-1}x^{m-1}+a_{m-2}x^{m-2}+\dots$ ($a_m\ne0$, $m\ge2$) has only real roots $w_1,\dots,w_m$ (with multiplicity), then $a_{m-1}^2-2a_ma_{m-2}\ge0$.

*Proof.* By Vieta, $\sum w_i=-\frac{a_{m-1}}{a_m}$ and $\sum_{i<j}w_iw_j=\frac{a_{m-2}}{a_m}$, so
$$0\le\sum w_i^2=\Big(\sum w_i\Big)^2-2\sum_{i<j}w_iw_j=\frac{a_{m-1}^2-2a_ma_{m-2}}{a_m^2}.\ \square$$

Let $p(x)=ax^k+bx^{k-1}+cx^{k-2}+\dots$ with $a\ne0$, $k\ge1$ (if $k=1$, $c=0$). Using $(x+1)^n=x^n+nx^{n-1}+\binom n2x^{n-2}+\dots$ and
$$p(x+1)=ax^k+(ka+b)x^{k-1}+\Big(\tbinom k2a+(k-1)b+c\Big)x^{k-2}+\dots,$$
we get $q_n(x)=A_nx^{n+k}+B_nx^{n+k-1}+C_nx^{n+k-2}+\dots$ with
$$A_n=2a,\qquad B_n=(n+k)a+2b,\qquad C_n=\Big(\tbinom n2+\tbinom k2\Big)a+(n+k-1)b+2c .$$
So $q_n$ has degree exactly $n+k\ge2$, and
$$B_n^2-2A_nC_n=a^2\big((n+k)^2-2n(n-1)-2k(k-1)\big)+4ab+4b^2-8ac,$$
that is,
$$B_n^2-2A_nC_n=a^2\big(-n^2+2(k+1)n-k^2+2k\big)+4ab+4b^2-8ac .$$
Since $a^2>0$, this tends to $-\infty$ as $n\to\infty$, so it is negative for all large $n$. By the Lemma, for those $n$ the polynomial $q_n$ has a non-real root. Hence only finitely many $n$ give a $q_n$ with all roots real. ∎

prompt:
Define the sequence $A_1,A_2,\dots$ of matrices by the following recurrence:
$$A_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad A_{n+1}=\begin{pmatrix}A_n&I_{2^n}\\I_{2^n}&A_n\end{pmatrix}\quad(n=1,2,\dots)$$
where $I_m$ is the $m\times m$ identity matrix.

Prove that $A_n$ has $n+1$ distinct integer eigenvalues $\lambda_0<\lambda_1<\dots<\lambda_n$ with multiplicities $\binom n0,\binom n1,\dots,\binom nn$, respectively.
answer: The eigenvalues are $\lambda_j=-n+2j$ with multiplicity $\binom nj$: if $A_nv=\lambda v$ then $\binom{v}{\pm v}$ are eigenvectors of $A_{n+1}$ for $\lambda\pm1$, and Pascal's rule propagates the multiplicities. ($A_n$ is the adjacency matrix of the $n$-cube.)

solutions.title: Induction with block eigenvectors
solutions.body:
We prove by induction that $A_n$ is symmetric and has an orthogonal basis of eigenvectors in which the eigenvalue $n-2j$ occurs exactly $\binom nj$ times ($j=0,\dots,n$).

For $n=1$: $A_1$ is symmetric with eigenvectors $(1,1)^T$, $(1,-1)^T$ for eigenvalues $1,-1$; multiplicities $\binom10,\binom11$.

Step: let $v_1,\dots,v_N$ ($N=2^n$) be an orthogonal eigenbasis of the symmetric matrix $A_n$, $A_nv_i=\mu_iv_i$. Then
$$A_{n+1}\begin{pmatrix}v_i\\v_i\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}A_nv_i+v_i\\v_i+A_nv_i\end{pmatrix}=(\mu_i+1)\begin{pmatrix}v_i\\v_i\end{pmatrix},\qquad A_{n+1}\begin{pmatrix}v_i\\-v_i\end{pmatrix}=(\mu_i-1)\begin{pmatrix}v_i\\-v_i\end{pmatrix}.$$
These $2N$ vectors are non-zero and pairwise orthogonal, hence an eigenbasis of $A_{n+1}$ (which is clearly symmetric). So the eigenvalues of $A_{n+1}$ are the numbers $\mu\pm1$, $\mu$ running over the eigenvalues of $A_n$ with multiplicity. The value $(n+1)-2j$ arises as $(n-2j)+1$ and as $(n-2(j-1))-1$, so its multiplicity is
$$\binom nj+\binom n{j-1}=\binom{n+1}j .$$
Thus $A_n$ has the $n+1$ distinct integer eigenvalues $\lambda_j=-n+2j$ ($\lambda_0<\dots<\lambda_n$), and $\lambda_j=n-2(n-j)$ has multiplicity $\binom n{n-j}=\binom nj$. ∎

solutions.title: Characters of the hypercube
solutions.body:
Index rows and columns of $A_n$ by $x\in\{0,1,\dots,2^n-1\}$, identified with binary vectors in $\{0,1\}^n$. By induction, $(A_n)_{xy}=1$ iff $x$ and $y$ differ in exactly one bit, and $0$ otherwise: for $n=1$ this is clear, and in $A_{n+1}$ the two diagonal blocks connect indices with the same top bit differing in one lower bit, while the identity blocks connect $x$ with $x+2^n$, which differ exactly in the top bit. So $A_n$ is the adjacency matrix of the $n$-dimensional cube.

For $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}$ let $\chi_S(x)=(-1)^{\sum_{i\in S}x_i}$. Writing $e_i$ for the $i$-th unit vector and $\oplus$ for bitwise addition mod 2,
$$(A_n\chi_S)(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n\chi_S(x\oplus e_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^{[i\in S]}\chi_S(x)=(n-2|S|)\,\chi_S(x).$$
The $2^n$ vectors $\chi_S$ are pairwise orthogonal ($\sum_x\chi_S(x)\chi_T(x)=\sum_x\chi_{S\triangle T}(x)=0$ for $S\ne T$), hence form an eigenbasis. Therefore the eigenvalues are $n-2|S|$, and $n-2j$ occurs $\#\{S:|S|=j\}=\binom nj$ times: $\lambda_j=-n+2j$ has multiplicity $\binom n{n-j}=\binom nj$. ∎

prompt:
Define the sequence $f_1,f_2,\dots\colon[0,1)\to\mathbb R$ of continuously differentiable functions by the following recurrence:
$$f_1=1;\qquad f'_{n+1}=f_nf_{n+1}\ \text{ on }(0,1),\qquad\text{and}\qquad f_{n+1}(0)=1.$$
Show that $\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(x)$ exists for every $x\in[0,1)$ and determine the limit function.

solutions.title: Monotone iteration and the fixed point
solutions.body:
**Formula.** The linear equation $y'=f_ny$, $y(0)=1$, has the unique solution
$$f_{n+1}(x)=\exp\Big(\int_0^xf_n(t)\,dt\Big).\tag{1}$$
Write $\Phi(g)(x)=\exp\big(\int_0^xg\big)$, so $f_{n+1}=\Phi(f_n)$. Clearly $g\le h$ on $[0,1)$ implies $\Phi(g)\le\Phi(h)$.

**Monotone and bounded.** $f_2(x)=e^x\ge1=f_1(x)$, and by monotonicity of $\Phi$, induction gives $f_n\le f_{n+1}$ for all $n$. Let $F(x)=\frac1{1-x}$; since $\int_0^x\frac{dt}{1-t}=-\ln(1-x)$, we have $\Phi(F)=F$. As $f_1=1\le F$, induction gives $f_n\le F$ for all $n$. So for every $x\in[0,1)$ the sequence $f_n(x)$ is non-decreasing and bounded by $\frac1{1-x}$, hence converges; call the limit $g(x)$. We have $1\le g\le F$.

**The limit is a fixed point.** Fix $x\in[0,1)$. On $[0,x]$ the functions $f_n$ increase to $g$ and are bounded by $\frac1{1-x}$, so by the monotone convergence theorem $\int_0^xf_n\to\int_0^xg$ (each $f_n$, by (1), is non-decreasing in $x$, so $g$ is non-decreasing and Riemann integrable as well). Letting $n\to\infty$ in (1):
$$g(x)=\exp\Big(\int_0^xg(t)\,dt\Big)\qquad(0\le x<1).$$

**Solve.** $G(x)=\int_0^xg$ is continuous ($g$ is locally bounded), so $g=e^{G}$ is continuous, hence $G$ is $C^1$ with $G'=e^{G}$, $G(0)=0$. Then $\big(e^{-G}\big)'=-G'e^{-G}=-1$, so $e^{-G(x)}=1-x$ and
$$g(x)=e^{G(x)}=\frac1{1-x}.$$

**Answer:** the limit exists for every $x\in[0,1)$ and $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}f_n(x)=\frac1{1-x}$. ∎

prompt:
Let $K$ be an equilateral triangle in the plane. Prove that for every $p>0$ there exists an $\varepsilon>0$ with the following property: If $n$ is a positive integer, and $T_1,\dots,T_n$ are non-overlapping triangles inside $K$ such that each of them is homothetic to $K$ with a negative ratio, and
$$\sum_{\ell=1}^n\operatorname{area}(T_\ell)>\operatorname{area}(K)-\varepsilon,$$
then
$$\sum_{\ell=1}^n\operatorname{perimeter}(T_\ell)>p.$$
answer: After an affine map, $K=\{x,y\ge0,\ x+y\le1\}$ and $T_i$ has vertical sections of length $t-L_i$ on $[L_i,L_i+s_i]$. The total section length $f(t)\le1-t$ satisfies $f(T)=\int_0^TN-\sum_{R_i\le T}s_i$ with $N(t)\ge f(t)/t$; if the uncovered area is $<\varepsilon'$ then $\sum s_i\ge\frac12\ln\frac1{2\delta}-\frac{\varepsilon'}\delta-\frac12\to\infty$ (with $\delta=\sqrt{\varepsilon'}$).

solutions.title: Vertical sections and a logarithmic lower bound
solutions.body:
**Normalisation.** An affine map multiplies all areas by the same constant and preserves homotheties and ratios of parallel lengths. Apply one taking $K$ to $K_0=\{(x,y):x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ x+y\le1\}$ (area $\frac12$). A homothety of $K_0$ with ratio $-s$ ($s>0$) gives a triangle
$$T=\{x\le a,\ y\le b,\ x+y\ge a+b-s\}$$
with vertices $(a,b),(a-s,b),(a,b-s)$. Since $T_\ell$ is homothetic to $K$ with ratio $-s_\ell$, $\operatorname{perimeter}(T_\ell)=s_\ell\operatorname{perimeter}(K)$, so it suffices to show: if the uncovered area of $K_0$ is less than $\varepsilon'$ (where $\varepsilon'$ is $\varepsilon$ times the area factor), then $\sum s_\ell\ge B(\varepsilon')$ for a bound $B(\varepsilon')\to\infty$ as $\varepsilon'\to0$.

**Vertical sections.** For $T_\ell$ put $L_\ell=a_\ell-s_\ell$ and $R_\ell=a_\ell$; $T_\ell\subseteq K_0$ gives $L_\ell\ge0$. The section of $T_\ell$ by the line $x=t$ has length
$$f_\ell(t)=(t-L_\ell)\cdot\mathbf 1[L_\ell\le t<R_\ell],$$
rising with slope $1$ from $0$ to $s_\ell$ and then dropping by $s_\ell$ at $t=R_\ell$. Let $f=\sum_\ell f_\ell$ and $N(u)=\#\{\ell:L_\ell<u<R_\ell\}$. Checking the three cases $t<L_\ell$, $L_\ell\le t<R_\ell$, $t\ge R_\ell$ gives $f_\ell(t)=\int_0^t\mathbf 1[L_\ell<u<R_\ell]\,du-s_\ell\mathbf 1[R_\ell\le t]$, so
$$f(t)=\int_0^tN(u)\,du-\sum_{R_\ell\le t}s_\ell .\tag{1}$$
Three facts (each for all $t$ outside the finitely many $L_\ell,R_\ell$):
* $f(t)\le1-t$: for $L_\ell<t<R_\ell$ the open section of $T_\ell$ lies in the interior of $T_\ell$, so the sections of different triangles do not overlap, and they lie in the section of $K_0$, of length $1-t$.
* $f(t)\le t\,N(t)$, because each active triangle has $f_\ell(t)=t-L_\ell\le t$.
* $\int_0^1f=\sum\frac{s_\ell^2}2=\sum\operatorname{area}(T_\ell)$. So with $D(t)=1-t-f(t)\ge0$ (the uncovered length), $\int_0^1D<\varepsilon'$.

**Estimate.** Let $0<\delta\le\frac12$. Using $N(u)\ge\frac{f(u)}u=\frac{1-u-D(u)}u$, $1-u\ge\frac12$ on $[\delta,\frac12]$, and $\frac{D(u)}u\le\frac{D(u)}\delta$:
$$\int_0^{1/2}N(u)\,du\ge\int_\delta^{1/2}\frac{du}{2u}-\frac1\delta\int_0^1D\ge\frac12\ln\frac1{2\delta}-\frac{\varepsilon'}\delta .$$
By (1) with $t=\frac12$ and $f(\frac12)\le\frac12$,
$$\sum_\ell s_\ell\ \ge\sum_{R_\ell\le1/2}s_\ell=\int_0^{1/2}N-f\big(\tfrac12\big)\ge\frac12\ln\frac1{2\delta}-\frac{\varepsilon'}{\delta}-\frac12 .$$
Choosing $\delta=\sqrt{\varepsilon'}$ (for $\varepsilon'\le\frac14$):
$$\sum_\ell s_\ell\ge B(\varepsilon'):=\frac12\ln\frac1{2\sqrt{\varepsilon'}}-\sqrt{\varepsilon'}-\frac12\ \xrightarrow[\varepsilon'\to0]{}\ \infty .$$

**Conclusion.** Given $p>0$, choose $\varepsilon>0$ so small that $B(\varepsilon')\operatorname{perimeter}(K)>p$. Then whenever the $T_\ell$ cover more than $\operatorname{area}(K)-\varepsilon$, we get $\sum\operatorname{perimeter}(T_\ell)=\operatorname{perimeter}(K)\sum s_\ell>p$. ∎
